'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''anat.'', a transversalis or transversus: as, the ''transverse'' of the abdomen, perineum, or sole of the foot.

'''transverse''' (trâns-vėrs′), ''adv.'' [< ''transverse'', ''a.''] Crosswise; across; transversely.

{{smaller block|A violent cross wind from either coast
Blows them ''transverse'' ten thousand leagues awry.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 487.}}}}

'''transverse''' (trâns-vėrs′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''transversed'', ppr. ''transversing''. [< ME. ''transversen'', < OF. *''transverser'', ''traverser'', < ML. ''transversare'', go across, transgress, traverse, < L. ''transversus'',
readings.c4s2:
pp. of ''transvertere'', turn across, turn away: see ''transverse'', ''a.'' Cf. ''traverse'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To overturn; turn topsyturvy.

{{smaller block|And though our Monarchy be quite ''transverst'',
And we as slaues through the wide world disperst,
'Tis not because we put to heauy doome
The great Messias.
{{right|''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 284.}}}}

'''2.''' To change; transpose. Compare ''transprose''.

{{smaller block|If there be any Wit in 't, as there is no Book but has some, I ''Transverse'' it: that is, if it be Prose, put it into Verse, . . . if it be Verse, put it into Prose.
{{right|''Buckingham'', The Rehearsal, i. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To transgress; run counter.

{{smaller block|Ac treuthe, that trespassede neuere ne ''transuersede'' aȝens the lawe,
Bote lyuede as his lawe tauhte.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xv. 209.}}}}

[Rare in all uses.]

'''transverse-cubital''' (trȧns-vėrs′kū″bi-ta̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''transversocubital''.

'''transversely''' (trȧns-vėrs′li), ''adv.'' In a transverse position, direction, or manner; crosswise.

{{smaller block|At Stonehenge the stones lie ''transversely'' upon each other.
{{right|''Stillingfleet.''}}}}

'''transverse-medial''' (trȧns-vėrs′mē″di-a̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''transversomedial''.
readings.c4s3:
¶
'''transverse-quadrate''' (trȧns-vėrs′kwod″rāt), ''a.'' In ''entom.'', having approximately the form of a rectangular parallelogram, which is broader than it is long.

'''transversi''', ''n.'' Plural of ''transversus''.

'''transversion''' (trȧns-vėr′shon), ''n.'' [< ML. ''transversio''(''n''-), < L. ''transvertere'', turn across: see ''transverse'', ''a.'' and ''v.''] The act or process of transversing. See ''transverse'', ''v.''

{{smaller block|My first Rule is the Rule of ''Transversion'', or Regula Duplex, changing Verse into Prose, or Prose into Verse.
{{right|''Buckingham'', The Rehearsal, i. 1.}}}}

'''transverso-analis''' (trȧns-vėr″sō-ạ̄-nā′lis), ''n.'' [NL.: see ''transverse'' and ''anal.''] Same as ''transversus perinæi'' (which see, under ''transversus'').

'''transversocubital''' (trȧns-vėr-sō-kū′bi-tạl), ''a.'' [As ''transverse'' + ''cubital.''] Running across and dividing the cubital cells of the wings of some insects: noting certain nervures.

'''transversomedial''' (trȧns-vėr-sọ̄-mē′di-ạl), ''a.'' [As ''transverse'' + ''medial.''] Crossing the medial cells of the wings of some insects, as hymenopters: noting certain nervures.

'''transversospinalis''' (trȧns-vėr″sō-spī-nā′lis), ''n.''; pl. ''transversospinales'' (-lēz). [NL.: see ''transverse'' and ''spinal.''] One of the set or series of spinal muscles which connect the transverse with the spinous processes of vertebræ.

'''transversovertical''' (trȧns-vėr″sō-vėr′ti-kạl), ''a.'' [As ''transverse'' + ''vertical.''] Relating to what is transverse and vertical.—{{smaller|'''Transversovertical index''', the ratio of the greatest height to the greatest breadth of the cranium.}}
readings.c4s4:
¶
'''transversum''' (trȧns-vėr′sum), ''n.''; pl. ''transversa'' (-sä̤). [NL., prop. neut. of L. ''transversus'', transverse: see ''transverse''.] In ''herpet.'', the transverse bone of the skull: more fully called ''os transversum''. See ''transverse'', ''a.'', 5 (with cut).

Same as ''lateral vibration'' (which see, under ''lateral'').}} '''II.''' ''n.'' In ''anat.'', a transversalis or transversus: as, the ''transverse'' of the abdomen, perineum, or sole of the foot.
